§0Part A · organisation

Organisation of the musculoskeletal system

One framework doing five jobs — then split into a protective core and a mobile periphery.

The skeletal system is far more than a coat-rack for muscle. It has five primary functions, and the way the skeleton is divided into two regions maps directly onto those jobs.

The five jobs of the skeleton

  • Support — bears the body's weight and gives soft tissues a framework to attach to.
  • Storage — a reservoir of minerals (calcium, phosphate) and lipids (yellow marrow).
  • Blood cell production — haematopoiesis in red marrow.
  • Protection — hard cases around soft organs (skull, thoracic cage, vertebral canal).
  • Leverage — bones act as levers, changing the magnitude and direction of muscle force.

§0.1Axial vs appendicular skeleton

The 206 adult bones split into two divisions whose names announce their jobs.

The two divisions of the skeleton
DivisionWhat's in itBonesJob
AxialSkull, vertebral column, sacrum & coccyx, thoracic cage80The central axis — protection of organs
AppendicularUpper limbs + shoulder girdle, lower limbs + pelvic girdle126Attaches limbs to the axis — movement
Memory hook · axial vs appendicular

Axial = the axis (the central pole: head + spine + ribcage). Appendicular = the appendages (the bits that hang off — arms and legs plus the girdles that bolt them on). 80 + 126 = 206.

§0.2Upper vs lower limbs — built for opposite jobs

Both are appendicular, but they're specialised in opposite directions.

  • Upper limbs — a great range of movement and the ability to grasp and manipulate. Mobility is prioritised over stability.
  • Lower limbs — support body weight, move the body from place to place, and maintain equilibrium (balance). Stability is prioritised over mobility.
Reasoning · why "levers" is the key idea

A muscle can only pull, and only over a short distance. Attach that pull to a rigid bar (bone) pivoting at a joint and you convert a small, strong contraction into a large, fast movement at the far end — or trade speed for force. That's why the same muscular effort can either hurl a ball or hold a heavy weight: the lever geometry decides. Keep this in mind for §2 — joint shape sets the lever's range.

§1Part A · bones

Bones — classification & markings

Two ways to sort 206 bones, and a vocabulary for every bump and hole on them.

The adult skeleton has 206 major bones, classified two ways: by their internal tissue organisation and by their shape.

By tissue organisation

  • Compact (cortical) bone — dense outer shell; strong against bending & torsion.
  • Spongy (cancellous / trabecular) bone — a lattice of struts; light, and houses marrow. (Revise the bone histology module on iLearn.)

§1.1By shape

As Plate 1.1 lays out, bones sort into five shape classes — and shape follows function.

Label Key — five shape classes
Long
Longer than wide, with a shaft & two ends (e.g. femur, humerus). Function: leverage for movement.
Short
Roughly cube-shaped (carpals, tarsals). Function: stability with limited gliding.
Flat
Thin, often curved (skull, sternum, ribs). Function: protection and broad muscle attachment.
Irregular
Complex shapes that fit no other class (vertebrae, facial bones). Function: protection & varied attachment.
Sesamoid
Small bones embedded within tendons (patella). Function: protect the tendon & improve its leverage.

§1.2Anatomy of a long bone

Plate 1.2 shows the parts of a long bone — the reference model for the whole class.

Label Key — the long-bone regions
Diaphysis
The shaft — a tube of compact bone around the medullary (marrow) cavity.
Epiphysis
The expanded end — spongy bone under a compact shell; forms the joint surface.
Metaphysis
The zone between diaphysis and epiphysis; contains the growth (epiphyseal) plate in the young.
Medullary cavity
Central space holding marrow (red = blood cell production; yellow = fat).

§1.3Bone markings — the vocabulary

Every bump, ridge and hole has a name, and the name tells you what happens there: a place where something attaches, articulates, or passes through.

Projections for muscle / ligament attachment
TermMeaning
ProcessAny projection or bump
TrochanterA large, rough projection (only on the femur)
Tuberosity / tubercleA smaller rough projection
Crest / lineA prominent ridge / a low ridge
SpineA pointed, narrow process
RamusAn arm of bone that angles off the main structure
Articular surfaces & openings
TermMeaning
HeadExpanded articular end, set off by a neck
CondyleA smooth, rounded articular process
TrochleaA smooth, grooved (pulley-like) articular process
FacetA small, flat articular surface
Fossa / sulcusA shallow depression / a narrow groove
Foramen / canal / meatusA hole / channel / passage for vessels & nerves
SinusAn air-filled chamber within a bone
Memory hook · sort by the "-ity" of the surface

If a marking is rough, a muscle or tendon pulls there (tuberosity, trochanter, crest). If it's smooth, it slides against another bone (condyle, facet, trochlea). If it's a hole, something passes through (foramen, canal, meatus).

§2Part A · joints

Joints (articulations)

Two ways to classify a join: by how much it moves, and by what holds it together.

A joint (articulation) is wherever two bones meet. Joints are classified functionally (by movement) and structurally (by the tissue between the bones). The two schemes overlap — structure sets the possible movement.

§2.1Functional classification — by movement

Functional classes
ClassMovementExample
SynarthrosisNo movementSkull sutures
AmphiarthrosisSlight movementPubic symphysis, intervertebral discs
DiarthrosisFree movementAll synovial joints (knee, shoulder)

§2.2Structural classification — by what binds the bones

The criteria are the presence/absence of a synovial cavity and the type of connective tissue holding the bones together. Plate 2.1 shows the fibrous and cartilaginous families.

Label Key — the three structural families
Fibrous
No cavity; bones held by dense connective tissue. Subtypes: sutures (skull), syndesmoses (tibia–fibula), interosseous membranes.
Cartilaginous
No cavity; bones held by cartilage. Subtypes: synchondroses (primary — hyaline, e.g. growth plate) and symphyses (secondary — fibrocartilage, e.g. pubic symphysis).
Synovial
Cavity present; bones enclosed by an articular capsule (with accessory ligaments). The freely-movable joints — decoded next.

§2.3The six synovial joints

Synovial joints are the movers. Their shape sets their range — as Plate 2.2 shows, six geometries give six movement repertoires.

Label Key — shape → example → movement
Planar (gliding)
Flat surfaces; intercarpal joints. Short gliding/sliding movements.
Hinge
Convex into concave; elbow, knee. Movement in one plane (flexion/extension).
Pivot
A round process in a ring; atlanto-axial (C1–C2), proximal radio-ulnar. Rotation.
Condyloid (ellipsoid)
Oval condyle in an oval socket; wrist (radiocarpal). Two planes (no rotation).
Saddle
Reciprocal saddle surfaces; thumb carpometacarpal. Two planes + a little rotation — enables opposition.
Ball-and-socket
Ball in a cup; shoulder, hip. Movement in all planes (the freest).
Reasoning · why "structure permits movement"

Trace it on Plate 2.2: a hinge is two matched cylinders, so it can only roll one way — one plane of motion. A ball-and-socket removes those constraints, so it swings in every plane but pays for it in stability (why the shoulder dislocates and the suture never does). The joint's geometry is its function — you can predict the movement from the shape alone.

§3Part A · muscle

Muscle

~700 engines that only pull — organised, attached and coordinated to move levers.

The muscular system is roughly 700 skeletal muscles. Its primary job is to produce movement, but it also maintains posture and body position, supports soft tissues, forms sphincters, generates heat, and stores nutrients.

Five properties of muscle tissue

  • Excitability — responds to nerve stimulation.
  • Contractility — shortens when stimulated.
  • Extensibility — can be stretched without damage.
  • Elasticity — recoils to its resting shape.
  • Adaptability — remodels in response to use.
Label Key
Axial muscles
Move/stabilise the head & trunk (the axial skeleton).
Appendicular muscles
Move the limbs & girdles — the mirror of the skeletal division in §0.

§3.1Fascicle arrangement

Muscles are bundles of fascicles, and the way those bundles line up (Plate 3.2) trades off force against range.

Label Key — arrangements
Parallel
Fascicles run the muscle's length — big range of shortening.
Convergent
Broad origin narrowing to one tendon (pectoralis major) — versatile pull direction.
Pennate
Short fascicles angling onto a tendon — packs in more fibres for more force. Unipennate (one side, extensor digitorum longus), bipennate (both sides, rectus femoris), multipennate (many directions, deltoid).
Circular
Fascicles in rings — the sphincters that close an opening.

§3.2Origin, insertion & attachments

Every muscle spans a joint from a fixed point to a moving one (Plate 3.3).

Label Key
Origin
Attachment to the stationary bone — usually the proximal end.
Insertion
Attachment to the movable bone — usually distal. (Some muscles reverse roles depending on which end is fixed.)

Supportive connective tissue

  • Tendon — a rope of connective tissue attaching muscle to bone.
  • Aponeurosis — a broad, flat sheet attaching muscle to muscle (or bone).
  • Fascia — fibrous sheets that wrap and compartmentalise. Superficial fascia carries superficial vessels, nerves & lymphatics; deep fascia forms compartments (e.g. brachial/antebrachial fascia; its thickenings at the wrist form the flexor and extensor retinacula).

§3.3Biotensegrity & coordination

Biotensegrity: bones don't stack like bricks — they float as compression struts suspended in a continuous tension network of myofascia & ligaments. Movement is a whole-system negotiation, and muscles work in defined roles:

  • Agonist (prime mover) — produces the movement.
  • Antagonist — opposes it (controls & smooths the motion).
  • Synergist — cancels unwanted motion, stabilises intermediate joints.
  • Fixator — stabilises the agonist's origin.
  • Muscle compartment — a group of muscles with a shared function, wrapped by fascia with their own neurovascular bundle.
Clinical / real-world · compartment syndrome

Because deep fascia forms a closed compartment, bleeding or swelling inside it (after a fracture or crush) has nowhere to go. Pressure rises, chokes off the compartment's own vessels and nerves, and the muscle dies — compartment syndrome, a surgical emergency. The anatomy of §3.2 is exactly why it happens.

§4Part B · development

How a limb is built

From a bump on the flank to a rotated, jointed limb — two mesoderms, one ridge, and well-timed cell death.

Human development is continuous from fertilisation: a sperm fertilises an oocyte to form a zygote (totipotent), which builds the whole body — and it doesn't stop at birth (teeth, the brain tripling in weight by ~16, most changes complete by ~25).

Label Key — the timeline
Prenatal → Embryonic
Fertilisation to week 8 — organs form (the vulnerable window for anomalies, §5).
Prenatal → Foetal
Week 9 to birth — growth & maturation of what's formed.
Postnatal
Newborn → infant → toddler → child → adolescent → adult.

§4.1Gastrulation & the germ layers

The key early event is gastrulation: the bilaminar disc becomes three primary germ layers — endoderm, mesoderm, ectoderm — each giving rise to specific tissues. The entire MSK system comes from mesoderm.

Adult derivatives of the three germ layers
EctodermMesodermEndoderm
Nervous system (brain, cord, peripheral nerves)MSK — bones, cartilage, tendons & all muscleEpithelial lining of the digestive tract
Epidermis & appendages (hair, nails, glands)Cardiovascular & lymphatic (heart, vessels, spleen)Accessory digestive organs (pancreas, liver, gallbladder)
Sensory organs; some glands (pituitary, adrenal medulla)Urogenital system (kidneys, gonads); dermis of skinRespiratory system; glands (thyroid, parathyroid, thymus)

§4.2The limb bud & its two mesoderms

Limb development starts at the end of week 4. As Plate 4.2 shows in cross-section, two regions of mesoderm feed the limb, and they divide the labour cleanly.

Label Key — division of labour
Lateral plate mesoderm (somatic)
Forms the limb's skeletal framework — bones & connective tissue.
Paraxial mesoderm (somite)
Supplies the muscular and vascular components (migrating myogenic cells).
Memory hook · which mesoderm makes what

Lateral Plate → the Platform (bones/skeleton). Somite → the Soft movers (skeletal muscle). This is exactly Learning Outcome 2 — be able to compare the two contributions.

The upper limb bud appears first (visible ~day 26), the lower ~2 days later. Each bud is a mesodermal core under ectoderm, capped by a thickened apical ectodermal ridge (AER) — see Plate 4.3.

Label Key
Mesenchymal core
Embryonic connective tissue (initially all lateral plate mesoderm) that condenses into cartilage models, then ossifies.
Ectoderm
The surface cover of the bud.
Apical ectodermal ridge (AER)
A thickened ridge at the bud's tip. It signals to the underlying mesoderm to keep growing outward, driving proximo-distal elongation.
Label Key
Paddle shape
The bud flattens into a paddle (the future hand/foot plate) before digits form.
AER (arrow)
Ridge along the paddle's rim; section shows the mesenchymal core (M) under the ectodermal ridge (E).
Reasoning · why the AER matters

Growth is directional: the limb must extend away from the body wall. The AER is the tip's growth-control centre — it keeps the mesoderm just beneath it dividing, so the limb lengthens shoulder-to-fingertip in order. Remove the AER experimentally and the limb truncates. It's the reason a limb grows out rather than just bulging.

§4.3Other migrating cells: somites & neural crest

The bud's mesenchyme is soon joined by migrants from elsewhere (Plate 4.5).

Label Key — who arrives and what they become
Somite (paraxial mesoderm)
Myogenic cells → the limb's skeletal muscle.
Neural crest cells
Detach from the neural tube and migrate in → Schwann cells, sensory neurons, and pigment cells (melanocytes).
Motor axons
Grow out from the neural tube (future brain & spinal cord) into the limb.

§4.4Somite subdivisions

Somites are paired blocks of mesenchyme flanking the neural tube. Each subdivides into three cell populations (Plate 4.6) that migrate to set destinations.

Label Key — one somite, three fates
Sclerotome
Migrates around the neural tube → vertebrae & ribs.
Myotome
→ skeletal muscle of neck, trunk & limbs.
Dermatome
→ dermis of the skin (connective tissue).
Memory hook · somite fates

Sclerotome → skeleton (hard: vertebrae/ribs). Myotome → muscle. Dermotome → dermis. The prefixes literally name the tissue.

Limb muscle specifically arises from myogenic cells of the myotome/dermomyotome of the somites — the muscle precursors migrate into the lateral-plate-derived skeletal scaffold.

§4.5Nerve supply, rotation & digits

Nerves: motor axons enter the limb bud in week 5, growing into dorsal & ventral muscle masses before those masses split into individual muscles; sensory axons follow; neural-crest-derived Schwann cells myelinate them.

Rotation (week 8): the limbs rotate into their adult positions — and the two limbs rotate in opposite directions (Plate 4.7).

Label Key
Upper limbs
Rotate dorsally (laterally) — so the extensor compartment ends up on the dorsal (back) side.
Lower limbs
Rotate ventrally (medially) — so the extensor compartment ends up on the ventral (front) side (why the knee and elbow point opposite ways).

Digits: the paddle-shaped hand/foot plate is sculpted by apoptosis — programmed cell death removes the tissue between the digital rays, freeing the fingers (Plate 4.8).

Label Key
Interdigital apoptosis
Programmed cell death (pale zones) between the rays — separates the digits. Failure here → syndactyly (§5).
Reasoning · building by subtraction

Fingers aren't grown outward one by one — the hand starts as a solid paddle and the webbing is deleted. It's cheaper to carve digits from a plate than to extend five separate buds, and it explains the commonest hand anomaly: if the deletion step fails, the fingers stay joined (syndactyly).

§5Part B · when it goes wrong

Limb anomalies

Each defect is a developmental step from §4 that failed — read them backwards to the mechanism.

Limb anomalies range from minor (common, harmless) to major (mostly genetic). Extremes: meromelia (partial absence of a limb) and amelia (absence of a whole limb). Causes are multiple: genetic factors & mutant genes, teratogens (drugs, alcohol, infections, radiation) in the first 8 weeks, mechanical pressure, and vascular disruption.

§5.1Digit anomalies — syndactyly & clefts

Label Key
Syndactyly
Failed interdigital apoptosis (§4.5). Cutaneous = soft-tissue web between digits; osseous = bones fused (digital-ray notches never formed).
Split hand/foot (cleft / "claw" hand)
Reduced digit number with a wide gap between anterior & posterior digits.
Label Key
Polydactyly
Supernumerary digits, usually undeveloped. Inherited as a genetic dominant trait.
Congenital clubfoot (talipes)
Multifactorial (genes + environment + abnormal intrauterine position), ~1:1000 births. Foot is abnormally positioned, preventing normal weight-bearing; talipes equinovarus is the commonest type.

§5.2Achondroplasia

The commonest genetic cause of disproportionate short stature (dwarfism) — see Plate 5.3.

Label Key — mechanism & features
Cause
Mutation in FGFR3; autosomal dominant (often a new mutation). It impairs the conversion of cartilage to bone in the limbs & skull.
Body proportions
Average-sized torso with shortened limbs.
Head/face
Macrocephaly, prominent forehead, undeveloped midface.
Other
Short broad fingers, limited elbow extension; infantile hypotonia; spinal & foramen magnum stenosis.
Clinical / real-world · dominant, yet often "new"

Achondroplasia is autosomal dominant, so an affected parent has a 50% chance of passing it on — but most cases arise as a fresh (de novo) FGFR3 mutation in a child of average-height parents. When both parents are affected, a homozygous inheritance (¼ of children) is severe and lethal in utero — a classic Punnett-square teaching case.

§5.3Teratogens & the thalidomide tragedy

The embryonic period (first 8 weeks) is the vulnerable window — precisely when the signalling, apoptosis and tissue formation of §4 are happening. Thalidomide, marketed in the late 1950s–60s as a "safe" anti-nausea drug for morning sickness, caused catastrophic limb defects (meromelia/amelia) when taken in early pregnancy — the defining lesson in teratology.

Clinical / real-world · preconception care

Because the damage is done before many women know they're pregnant, prevention is preconception: plan the pregnancy, review chronic medications with a GP (swap teratogenic drugs for safer ones), and avoid alcohol, smoking and recreational drugs before and during pregnancy.

R Recall checklist — the whole lecture
  • Skeletal functions — support, mineral/lipid storage, blood cell production, protection, leverage.
  • Axial (80) = skull + spine + ribcage (protect); Appendicular (126) = limbs + girdles (move). Total 206.
  • Bone shapes — long, short, flat, irregular, sesamoid; tissue = compact vs spongy.
  • Joints functional — syn(none)/amphi(slight)/di(free); structural — fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial.
  • Six synovial — planar, hinge, pivot, condyloid, saddle, ball-and-socket (shape sets movement).
  • Muscle — ~700; properties E-C-E-E-A; fascicles parallel/convergent/pennate/circular; origin(fixed)/insertion(moved).
  • Germ layers — MSK is mesoderm. Limbs start end of wk4.
  • Lateral plate mesoderm → skeleton; somite (paraxial) → muscle; AER → outgrowth.
  • Somite → sclerotome (vertebrae/ribs), myotome (muscle), dermatome (dermis).
  • Timeline — motor axons wk5, joints wk6–8, rotation wk8 (upper dorsal, lower ventral), digits by apoptosis.
  • Anomalies — syndactyly (failed apoptosis), polydactyly (dominant), clubfoot (~1:1000), achondroplasia (FGFR3, AD), thalidomide (teratogen).
